```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r attach}
library(mysterymodel)
```

A nomogram is a published instrument. Someone will read risks off it for real
patients, by hand, years after the code that drew it stopped running. So the
question `mm_nomogram()` answers is not "did `rms` draw something" but "does
what it drew give the same answer as the model it was drawn from".

This article does by hand what `mm_nomogram()` does internally, because the
check is only convincing if you can see it.

```{r fit}
cohort <- mm_synthetic_cohort(n = 500, prevalence = 0.11, seed = 1978)

project <- mm_project("uds", "event",
                      c("age", "bmi", "sex", "prior_uti"),
                      positive_class = 1, cohort = cohort, seed = 1978)

model <- suppressWarnings(
  mm_model(project, cohort, nonlinear = "age",
           interactions = list(c("prior_uti", "sex"))))

nom <- mm_nomogram(model, out_dir = NULL)
nom
```

```{r plot, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6.5}
plot(nom$nomogram)
```

## An interaction makes one variable appear on several axes

```{r axes}
nom$axes
```

`sex` is not an axis. There are two axes that each hold both `sex` and
`prior_uti`, and they are mutually exclusive: a patient with no prior UTI reads
one, a patient with a prior UTI reads the other. A reader who gathered `sex`
ticks from a single axis would get half the model.

```{r axis-values}
mysterymodel:::mm_axis_values(nom$nomogram, project$predictors)
```

That is why the points reader gathers a predictor's tabulated values across
axes rather than off one, and why an axis contributes only when the profile
matches every categorical value the axis holds fixed. Exactly one of the two
applies to any patient, so nothing is counted twice and nothing is missed.

## Reading one patient, by hand

Take a 70 year old woman with a BMI of 31 and a prior UTI.

```{r patient}
patient <- data.frame(
  age       = 70,
  bmi       = 31,
  sex       = factor("female", levels = model$schema$predictors$sex$levels),
  prior_uti = factor("yes", levels = model$schema$predictors$prior_uti$levels)
)
```

Sum the points from every axis that applies:

```{r points}
total <- unname(mysterymodel:::mm_nomogram_points(nom$nomogram, patient))
total
```

Convert the total to the linear predictor using the printed scale, then to a
risk:

```{r read}
lp <- mysterymodel:::mm_total_to_lp(nom$nomogram, total)
c(total_points = total, linear_predictor = lp, risk = plogis(lp))

unname(mysterymodel:::mm_nomogram_risk(nom$nomogram, patient))
```

Now ask the model the same question:

```{r compare}
mm_predict(model, patient)$.pred
```

Neither calculation consulted the other. The reader above touched only
`nom$nomogram`, a list of printed axis values; `mm_predict()` touched only the
fitted `lrm` object. That independence is what makes the agreement evidence
rather than a restatement.

```{r gap}
abs(unname(mysterymodel:::mm_nomogram_risk(nom$nomogram, patient)) -
    mm_predict(model, patient)$.pred)
```

## Every tick, not one patient

`mm_nomogram()` does not check a profile someone chose. It varies each
predictor over all of its tabulated ticks while the others sit at their first,
so every tick of every axis is exercised without taking the product of them
all:

```{r profiles}
profiles <- mysterymodel:::mm_tick_profiles(nom$nomogram, model)
nrow(profiles)
head(profiles)
```

Those profiles come back again in the next section, where one of them turns out
to be the reason the points-to-risk step is written the way it is.

```{r check-all}
read <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(profiles)), function(i)
  mysterymodel:::mm_nomogram_risk(nom$nomogram, profiles[i, , drop = FALSE]),
  numeric(1))
fitted <- mm_predict(model, profiles)$.pred

summary(abs(read - fitted))
nom$worst_disagreement
```

Machine precision, across a model with a spline and an interaction. If the
worst gap exceeded `tolerance`, `mm_nomogram()` would refuse to return at all:

```{r refuse, error = TRUE}
mm_nomogram(model, out_dir = NULL, tolerance = 1e-20)
```

That refusal is the whole design. An instrument that does not reproduce its own
model must not reach a manuscript, and the only moment anyone is in a position
to notice is the moment it is drawn.

## Why the points-to-risk step is a line and not an interpolation

The printed linear predictor axis is affine in total points, so the line
through it is the exact mapping:

```{r affine}
head(data.frame(points = nom$nomogram$lp$x,
                lp     = nom$nomogram$lp$x.real))
```

Interpolating between those ticks with clamped ends looks equivalent, and
inside the printed range it is. The axis does not start at zero points, though,
and nothing stops a patient from scoring below where it starts. Here is the
lowest-scoring profile this model admits, a 20 year old woman at the bottom of
the BMI range with no prior UTI:

```{r lowest}
totals <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(profiles)), function(i)
  unname(mysterymodel:::mm_nomogram_points(nom$nomogram,
                                           profiles[i, , drop = FALSE])),
  numeric(1))

lowest <- profiles[which.min(totals), , drop = FALSE]
lowest
min(totals)
min(nom$nomogram$lp$x)
```

Zero points, and the printed risk axis begins at 16.3. Clamped interpolation
has nowhere to go, so it returns the value at the lowest printed tick:

```{r clamped}
clamped <- approx(nom$nomogram$lp$x, nom$nomogram$lp$x.real,
                  xout = min(totals), rule = 2)$y
exact <- mysterymodel:::mm_total_to_lp(nom$nomogram, min(totals))

c(clamped_risk = plogis(clamped),
  exact_risk   = plogis(exact),
  model_risk   = mm_predict(model, lowest)$.pred)
```

A risk of 1.1% reported for a patient whose risk is 0.6%, with no warning and
nothing on the page to suggest the reading was out of range. That is the error
this package shipped in its own first nomogram reader, and it is why
`mm_total_to_lp()` uses the exact affine line instead and checks its linearity
rather than trusting it: the function errors if the axis deviates from affine by
more than 1e-8.

## Reading between ticks has a cost, and here it is

Everything above holds at the nomogram's own tabulated values. A clinician
reads between them, and a spline curves between printed ticks where linear
interpolation across them does not.

```{r reading-error}
nom$reading_error
```

That is a bound: no reading taken anywhere between the printed ticks can
differ from `mm_predict()` by more than that. It is a property of every printed
nomogram and of every clinician reading one, not a defect of this package, and
reporting its size is the alternative to leaving it unexamined.

The bound needs no search over combinations of predictors, because the error
decomposes. Total points are additive and the printed risk axis is affine in
them, so the discrepancy is the points-to-lp slope times the sum of each axis's
own interpolation error, and each of those is zero at that axis's ticks. So the
extremes of the sum are the sums of the extremes, one scan per axis finds them,
and the worst total goes through the steepest part of the logistic curve:

```{r reading-error-parts}
nom$reading_error_by_axis
c(lp_bound = nom$reading_error_lp,
  risk_bound = nom$reading_error,
  by_hand = unname(stats::plogis(nom$reading_error_lp / 2) -
                     stats::plogis(-nom$reading_error_lp / 2)))
```

`reading_error_by_axis` is where to look when the bound is too large for
comfort: it names the axis that needs more ticks. Fitting the same model
without the spline makes the whole thing vanish, because linear terms make the
printed points affine in the predictor and the interpolation exact:

```{r linear-model}
linear <- suppressWarnings(
  mm_model(project, cohort, interactions = list(c("prior_uti", "sex"))))
mm_nomogram(linear, out_dir = NULL)$reading_error
```

The claim is worth testing rather than taking on the arithmetic above. Three
hundred profiles drawn anywhere inside the printed axes, which is where a
clinician reads, and the worst gap any of them produces:

```{r reading-error-held}
ticks <- mysterymodel:::mm_axis_values(nom$nomogram, project$predictors)
set.seed(8)
anywhere <- data.frame(
  age = runif(300, min(ticks$age), max(ticks$age)),
  bmi = runif(300, min(ticks$bmi), max(ticks$bmi)),
  sex = factor(sample(model$schema$predictors$sex$levels, 300, TRUE),
               levels = model$schema$predictors$sex$levels),
  prior_uti = factor(sample(model$schema$predictors$prior_uti$levels, 300,
                            TRUE),
                     levels = model$schema$predictors$prior_uti$levels))
read_anywhere <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(anywhere)), function(i) unname(
  mysterymodel:::mm_nomogram_risk(nom$nomogram,
                                  anywhere[i, , drop = FALSE])), numeric(1))
c(worst_of_300 = max(abs(read_anywhere -
                           mm_predict(model, anywhere)$.pred)),
  bound = nom$reading_error)
```

## Readings that fall off the drawn scale

```{r off-axis}
nom$off_axis
range(nom$nomogram$lp$x)
```

A total outside the printed range is a reading a clinician cannot take, however
well the arithmetic behind it works. Those profiles are counted rather than
quietly reported as the nearest printed tick.

```{r off-axis-direct}
mysterymodel:::mm_off_axis(nom$nomogram, c(min(totals), total, 500))
```

## Exporting

```{r export}
out <- file.path(tempdir(), "nomogram-article")
drawn <- mm_nomogram(model, out_dir = out, width = 13, height = 9)
basename(drawn$files)
```

The landscape shape is the default because that is what the specification asks
for. The PDF is always written; the SVG and PNG follow when `svglite` and
`ragg` are installed, which is why they are suggested rather than required
dependencies.

```{r fingerprint}
identical(drawn$fingerprint, model$fingerprint)
```

The fingerprint is the fit's, so a figure in a manuscript can be tied to the
coefficients that produced it. A nomogram whose fingerprint does not match the
model table beside it was drawn from a different fit.
